description: We are a two-member Computer Science and Engineering team passionate about technology and space exploration. Our experience includes AI/ML, software development, web apps, and interactive simulations. Through hackathons, we have strengthened our research, problem-solving, and prototyping skills. At NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to combine our skills and creativity to develop useful solutions for key challenges in Earth and space science.
summary: AstraTerra is an interactive atlas that uses open elevation and surface-temperature data to help people find and evaluate Earth analogs for lunar and Martian exploration. In Terraform, choose a planetary region to rank 18 Earth sites by terrain relief, steepness and roughness. Each match shows its evidence and source, and a draggable divider compares the Earth and destination maps. In Explore, complete a Mars or lunar mission by comparing gravity, recording temperature evidence and testing suit protection or inspecting a candidate site. In Research, inspect individual terrain cells, switch map layers and export results. In the bundled catalog, Antarctica’s McMurdo Dry Valleys ranked first for Shackleton, with its strongest component in terrain roughness. The rankings can guide field-test shortlists. Differences in scale, gravity, atmosphere, temperature and radiation still matter when planning a mission.
details:
The challenge

Mission teams need Earth locations to test instruments, rover routes, sampling and field operations before deploying them on the Moon or Mars. Different analog sites help test different conditions: lava fields for broken volcanic terrain or polar valleys for isolated, uneven environments.

NASA’s challenge asks participants to use open data to identify these relationships and present them through maps, visualizations or tools. Team Red Shift built AstraTerra, combining destination mapping, ranked Earth analogs, a 3D mission lab and a research workspace.

What we built

AstraTerra compares 18 Earth terrain windows with six Moon and Mars regions. Lunar regions include Shackleton, Marius Hills and Mare Tranquillitatis. Mars regions include Jezero’s western delta and two Gale Crater areas.

The Earth catalog covers polar terrain, deserts, volcanic fields, impact craters and lava-cave-associated sites, including McMurdo Dry Valleys, Yungay, Death Valley, Meteor Crater, Nördlinger Ries, Lake Salda, Timanfaya, Kīlauea Iki and Lava Beds.

The app scores mapped surface windows, not underground caves. It supports three user levels: visitors can discover Earth matches, students can complete controlled missions, and reviewers can inspect measurements and export analyses. Recommendations include terrain sources and, where available, field research links.

Terraform · Map the surface and find Earth analogs

  1. Open Terraform, select Mars or Moon, and choose a destination such as South Pole: Shackleton.
  2. Explore Elevation, Slope and Roughness layers. Click the map to inspect individual terrain cells.
  3. Review ranked Earth candidates and select a site to see its overall and individual scores. Open Terrain source and Field research source for supporting information.
  4. Drag the divider between Earth and planetary maps to compare elevation, slope or roughness. Keyboard controls are also supported.
  5. Open Advanced maps, weights and export to adjust the importance of terrain features for different field exercises.

This workflow makes recommendations transparent. A site may score well in slope but poorly in roughness or elevation variability, helping users choose suitable field exercises.

How the ranking works

Digital elevation models represent surface heights as grids. AstraTerra processes selected terrain windows and calculates three main measurement groups:

  • Relief and elevation variability: Measures the height difference and distribution of elevations within a window.
  • Steepness: The Horn method estimates slope using neighboring elevation values. Scores consider average slope and the 90th percentile.
  • Roughness: The Riley Terrain Ruggedness Index measures elevation differences between neighboring cells.

Each component receives a score from 0–100. The overall index uses weighted averages: approximately 29% relief and elevation variability, 36% slope and 36% roughness after excluding temperature and rescaling.

Temperature remains visible where data exists but is excluded from ranking because Earth and planetary observations represent different measurement conditions. Users can adjust weights and examine their effects.

The final score is an exploratory terrain comparison, not a prediction of landing success or operational safety.

Findings and applications

Shackleton, lunar south pole

  • Top-ranked Earth site: McMurdo Dry Valleys
  • Overall similarity: 56.82/100
  • Roughness score: 69.15/100
  • Key finding: Offers a candidate for uneven-terrain route planning tests.

Gale Crater, Murray Buttes

  • Top-ranked Earth site: Mauna Kea
  • Overall similarity: 84.23/100
  • Roughness score: 90.97/100
  • Slope score: 83.46/100
  • Key finding: Supports traverse comparisons.

Mare Tranquillitatis

  • Top-ranked Earth site: Lava Beds, California
  • Overall similarity: 54.08/100
  • Slope score: 86.34/100
  • Key finding: Offers a starting point for volcanic terrain studies.

Jezero western delta

  • Top-ranked Earth site: Nördlinger Ries
  • Overall similarity: 35.25/100
  • Key finding: High slope similarity but lower overall similarity highlights differences in relief and ruggedness.

These results use the default catalog and weights. McMurdo and Mauna Kea are established analog sites. AstraTerra adds an inspectable comparison method for screening terrain windows. Field measurements and mission-specific engineering checks are still required before selecting operational test sites.

Explore · Complete a comparative mission

Atacama to Mars: Open Explore, select the Mars mission and enter the 3D Comparative Science Lab. Repeat the same object drop from 12 meters on Earth and Mars. The modeled fall takes 1.56 seconds on Earth and 2.54 seconds on Mars.

The model assumes release from rest and ignores air resistance, allowing users to observe how gravity affects fall time and impact speed.

Next, open Atmospheric Pressure & Survival. Test Mars without an EVA suit and then with a pressurized suit. The simulation displays ambient pressure, oxygen partial pressure and a separate internal suit environment under stated life-support assumptions.

In Temperature Exposure, log evidence for both worlds. Earth displays satellite surface-temperature observations where available, while Mars shows a planetary reference and identifies missing local observations. Select Complete Mission to open the debrief.

McMurdo to Shackleton: Repeat the gravity experiment on Earth and the Moon, log thermal evidence and inspect a Shackleton candidate. Lunar elevation, slope and roughness help identify access and traverse considerations. Diviner provides polar thermal observations within its seasonal and local-time context.

Permanent-base assessment also requires evidence about illumination, communications, subsurface resources, radiation and ground-bearing conditions. The debrief keeps these gaps visible.

Research · Inspect evidence and export analysis

Open Research and select an Earth site and planetary destination. Explore available elevation, slope, roughness, temperature or similarity layers. Click terrain cells to inspect numerical values and units, and adjust heatmap opacity to view the underlying terrain.

Use comparison controls to examine terrain profiles and weights. Save Analysis downloads a JSON record, while Export Scientific Report provides the report.

Research allows reviewers to inspect steep areas, source resolution and individual measurements. Terraform compares regional summary statistics, while Research's similarity heatmap compares corresponding positions within selected terrain windows. These windows may cover different physical areas and do not share geographic coordinates.

Data sources and evidence limits

  • Earth: NASADEM and Copernicus GLO-30 provide elevation data. Copernicus also supplies supplementary terrain windows, including McMurdo and the 12 added Terraform sites. Terra and Aqua MODIS provide land surface temperature composites, with possible cloud and coverage gaps.
  • Moon: LRO LOLA provides elevation, while Diviner Polar Cumulative Products provide polar surface-temperature observations. These datasets use separate grids.
  • Mars: MGS MOLA provides regional topography, including coarse Jezero terrain. The USGS/NASA Gale merged elevation model supplies localized Gale terrain. Published planetary temperature references support the educational mission but do not provide local mapped measurements.

Terrain resolution affects recorded relief, slope and roughness. Regional datasets show broad features, while rover navigation and landing preparation may require finer imagery and field verification. Geology, dust, ice and radiation also require separate evidence.

Future improvements include comparing windows at similar physical extents and resolutions, testing different locations and weights, and adding compatible measurements.

Software and implementation

  • React, TypeScript and React Router: Build the interface and connect the three workspaces.
  • Leaflet: Provides interactive geographic maps. Browser Canvas renders terrain layers and comparison controls.
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber: Power the 3D mission scenes.
  • Node.js, GeoTIFF.js and Proj4js: Support raster processing, coordinate conversion and terrain metric preparation.
  • Vite: Builds the application. GSAP and Lenis support animations and scrolling, while Lucide provides icons.
  • GitHub and Render: Support source handoff and static-site deployment. The browser loads bundled JSON and calculates rankings locally. Analysis exports are downloaded locally, without requiring a database or specialized hardware.
  • Testing: Node tests and Chrome checks verify calculations and key workflows, including source links, map comparisons and Mars mission completion.
  • AI assistance: OpenAI Codex supported code review, implementation, debugging, testing and documentation. Source measurements are credited to their providers, with additional team AI usage covered in the separate SI disclosure.

Intended impact

AstraTerra makes planetary data accessible to the public and provides educators with a practical way to teach controlled experiments, map reading and evidence quality.

Exploration teams can use its catalog to identify potential analog sites, plan field exercises and understand the limitations of each comparison. From mapping and ranking to mission debriefs and exported analyses, the platform keeps the investigation transparent and traceable.
